doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Teaching jazz ensembles and Gordon Stanley at Juilliard
summary: How he teaches undergraduate and graduate classes, and his teacher Gordon Stanley's advice to slow down.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well you’ve done a lot of teaching over the years and you still do. Do you teach jazz per se or do you teach a lot of different courses?

I teach two ensemble courses, and that is undergraduate ensemble courses. There are all kinds of elective classes that the kids can take. But the ensemble classes are classes that give them a chance to learn about jazz. Most of them don’t know anything about jazz. But whatever they can do when they’re undergraduate people, they’re allowed to take this elective class. And when they come in I don’t know what instruments they’re going to play, it could be clarinet, alto, tenor, it could be a French horn, it could be a violin player, it could be an oboe player, flute player, anybody. And if we have a bass player and a drummer and a piano player what I do is I take the basic tunes that we all play and I teach those tunes. And I correct the wrong notes that are there and I try to give them the proper inflection or phrasing, and then I try to explain to them how to play on the harmonies. Some of them come away grasping the idea. I have to demonstrate an awful lot. I have to sit down at the piano and actually play. You just can’t write out notes and say, “Do this.” It has to be hands on. And sometimes I’ll take a saxophone player and the rhythm section and play with them. Ask the other piano player to stand up and look, and pay attention to what I’m doing. And when they come back they get a better sense of how to comp or how to voice a chord. They listen to it and then after the class I’m usually inundated with questions, because it takes the whole class for them to think of the kind of questions they want to ask. So I have to make myself available for them. And the testing isn’t just telling them to do something, it’s doing it and having them watch or listen or play along or try. I have to go from ten to ten sometimes just to be with the students. You know, ten o’clock in the morning to ten o’clock at night. Because if I close my doors well then I lose the students. So I keep the doors open so anyone that has questions they want to ask, they come in and ask. Then I have a graduate class that’s with students who already know how to play jazz, and I make them write. See the idea is the more they write the more they search, the more they search the better they get. It’s like if you work at something you really want you can’t help but increase your information. You can’t help it. And it’s the

same way they taught me at Juilliard. I had some excellent teachers. Gordon Stanley would give me pieces that I thought I’d never be able to play. And I’d get to like say after three weeks of playing and still wasn’t there, and he’d ask me to come out to his house. He lived in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania and I’d come out to his house. And he had private students. And I’d be up in the attic, in that hot attic, practicing on that dummy keyboard. Then when I’d come down and play for him he would correct all the things I was doing and he’d say, “Now slow it down. If you can play it slowly, you can play it fast.” See those things I never got from other teachers. He was my best teacher. He gave me information that nobody else would give, now I’m just giving it back. And it works. Because I’ve been there, this is almost the tenth year. And I have some people, Jesus you wouldn’t believe, when you hear this young kid Jeb Patton, you’ll know what I mean. He’s amazing. He plays everything. He plays from Bach to bop.
